content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
55	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
56	
57	## Requirements
58	
59	- Python 3.11 or newer
60	- no third-party runtime dependencies
61	
62	## Run the service
63	
64	```bash
65	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
66	```
67	
68	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
69	has bound the port.
70	
71	## HTTP API
72	
73	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
74	
75	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
76	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
77	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
78	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
79	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
80	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
81	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
82	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
83	
84	### Tenants and quotas
85	
86	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
87	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
88	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
89	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
90	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
91	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
92	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
93	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
94	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
95	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
96	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
97	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
98	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
99	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
100	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
101	
102	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
103	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
104	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
105	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
106	history and status queries, as well as the quota declaration and delete, the quota
107	read and remaining query, the price
108	declaration and price delete, the price read and the price change history, and the usage, bill, and
109	metrics queries. An empty
110	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
111	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
112	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
113	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
114	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
115	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
116	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
117	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
118	the usual `409 conflict`.
119	
120	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
121	hold:
122	
123	```http
124	PUT /quotas
125	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
126	X-Tenant-Id: acme
127	
128	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
129	```
130	
131	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
132	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
133	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
134	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Every quota
135	route requires a tenant: declaring, deleting, and reading without
136	`X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty one) is a `400 validation_error`, and an
137	unknown query parameter on the delete or the remaining query is rejected the
138	same way, with the message naming the offending parameter. The response is
139	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
140	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
141	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
142	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
143	
144	Besides the two limits a declaration may carry one optional `growth` object
145	naming an automatic expansion policy for each limited resource. A policy
146	names only the resources it covers, and a resource it omits is never raised
147	automatically. Each named resource must declare exactly a positive integer
148	`step` and a positive integer `cap`, and the cap must not be below the
149	resource's declared limit:
150	
151	```http
152	PUT /quotas
153	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-2
154	X-Tenant-Id: acme
155	
156	{"workflows":10,"executions":100,"growth":{"workflows":{"step":5,"cap":50},"executions":{"step":50,"cap":500}}}
157	```
158	
159	A missing field, an unknown field (inside the policy or beside it), a
160	non-object policy, a resource other than `workflows` or `executions`, or a
161	step or cap that is non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite is a
162	`400 validation_error`; a cap below the resource's declared limit is rejected
163	the same way. Every such rejection writes nothing. A declaration without
164	`growth` is byte-for-byte the two-limit request above; repeating a declaration
165	replaces limits and policy as a whole, so a declaration that names no `growth`
166	also drops the tenant's previous policy. The declaration response and the
167	quota read include the policy only when one is declared, with each entry
168	listing `step` before `cap` and resources in workflows-first order:
169	
170	```json
171	{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100,"growth":{"workflows":{"step":5,"cap":50},"executions":{"step":50,"cap":500}}}}
172	```
173	
174	```http
175	GET /quotas
176	X-Tenant-Id: acme
177	```
178	
179	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
180	when the tenant has declared none.
181	
182	A tenant can also remove the quota it declared, on the same path with the
183	`DELETE` method and the same calling shape as the other quota writes:
184	
185	```http
186	DELETE /quotas
187	Idempotency-Key: quota-delete-1
188	X-Tenant-Id: acme
189	
190	{}
191	```
192	
193	The body must be exactly an empty object; a non-empty or non-object body, an
194	unknown field, or a non-finite value is a `400 validation_error` that touches
195	no quota. The delete removes the declaration as a whole and leaves no partial
196	write, so a later read gives the same definite empty result as for a tenant
197	that never declared one: the delete response and every following read both
198	return `{"quota":null}`, and the remaining query lists neither resource —
199	neither limit, holding, nor remaining — and repeats with exactly the same
200	result. Deleting the quota of a tenant that never declared one returns that
201	same definite empty result rather than an error. The delete clears only the
202	declaration: it deletes no existing workflow or execution, and data already
203	held stays fully usable. It writes no metering record, so recorded usage
204	counts and bill conclusions already reached stay exactly as they were; later
205	writes simply run without a quota check until the tenant declares again.
206	
207	The delete follows the same idempotency rules as every other write: the
208	`Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same delete with the same
209	key returns the first result and performs no second removal, and reusing a
210	key for another operation — including a quota declaration — in the same
211	tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the tenant's quota unchanged. Quotas
212	are scoped per tenant like everything else: deleting one tenant's quota never
213	affects another tenant's declaration or remaining room. A missing or empty
214	tenant and a missing idempotency key are `400 validation_error`, and every
215	failed validation writes nothing — no quota row, no metering record, and no
216	price-table change history.
217	
218	A separate read-only entry point reports how much room the declared quota
219	leaves, with the same calling shape as the quota read:
220	
221	```http
222	GET /quotas/status
223	X-Tenant-Id: acme
224	```
225	
226	Each limited resource gives three numbers — the declared `limit`, the
227	`held` count the quota decision itself uses, and the `remaining` room, which
228	is simply limit minus holding — in that key order, with workflows first and
229	executions second; the same query repeats with the same ordering:
230	
231	```json
232	{"status":{"workflows":{"limit":10,"held":3,"remaining":7},"executions":{"limit":100,"held":12,"remaining":88}}}
233	```
234	
235	Lowering a limit below the current holding reports the `remaining` room
236	truthfully as a negative number; it is neither clamped to zero nor rejected.
237	A tenant that has never declared a quota gets the definite empty result
238	`{"status":null}`, listing neither resource. The query is strictly read-only:
239	it writes no metering record and changes no declared quota, usage, bill,
240	scheduling, approval, or replay conclusion, and another tenant's quota and
241	holdings are never visible and never influence the result. It requires a
242	tenant and accepts no query parameters: a missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id`
243	header, an unknown parameter (named in the error message), or a repeated
244	parameter is a `400 validation_error`, and these rejections write nothing.
245	
246	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the write is admitted
247	once the resource declares a growth policy that can make room: the declared
248	limit is raised in whole steps — the smallest number of `step` increments
249	that admits the write — never past the `cap` and never by a partial final
250	step, and the raised limit commits with the write in the same transaction,
251	so the request succeeds instead of returning a conflict. The expansion
252	changes only the declared limit: it writes no metering record, changes no
253	recorded usage count, and changes no bill conclusion already reached.
254	Repeating the same write with the same idempotency key returns the first
255	result without a second expansion, and reusing that key for another
256	operation is the usual `409 conflict`. Without a policy on the resource, or
257	when no whole-step raise within the cap can admit the write — including when
258	the cap already leaves no room for one more holding — the whole request is
259	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
260	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
261	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
262	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write and leaves the limit
263	untouched: nothing is inserted and previously stored data is unaffected,
264	exactly as for validation failures. The quota read and the remaining query
265	report the raised limit; the remaining query's `remaining` room is computed
266	from it.
267	
268	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
269	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
270	is at its execution limit, a growth policy raises the limit exactly as for a
271	manual creation and the period fires normally; when there is no policy or
272	the cap leaves no room a whole step can reach, the due period creates no
273	execution and the schedule is left unchanged — its cursor,
274	`last_triggered_at`, and `last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the
275	period is settled on a later pass once capacity exists, under the usual
276	per-period idempotence. Delivery history follows the tenant of the execution
277	it belongs to.
278	
279	### Tenant price tables
280	
281	The bill's baseline unit prices are built in. A tenant may instead declare
282	its own price table on a separate entry point with the same calling shape as
283	the quota declaration:
284	
285	```http
286	PUT /prices
287	Idempotency-Key: price-request-1
288	X-Tenant-Id: acme
289	
290	{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}
291	```
292	
293	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must be a non-empty
294	JSON object giving a map of metered action type to a positive-integer unit
295	price in cents. A non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite price,
296	an unknown metered type, a missing field (an empty object), an extra field
297	that is not a metered type, or a non-object body is a `400
298	validation_error` that writes nothing. Every price route requires a tenant:
299	declaring, deleting, and reading without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
300	one) is a `400 validation_error`, and an unknown query parameter on the
301	read or the delete is rejected the same way, with the message naming the
302	offending parameter. The response is
303	`{"prices":{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}}`, with the
304	declared types in ascending type-identifier order.
305	
306	A successful declaration replaces the tenant's price table as a whole with
307	exactly the types given this time; metered types the declaration does not
308	name fall back to the built-in default prices when a bill is taken. The
309	declaration rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken
310	before it was made.
311	
312	```http
313	GET /prices
314	X-Tenant-Id: acme
315	```
316	
317	Returns the price table currently declared by the tenant, in ascending
318	type-identifier order, or the definite empty result `{"prices":null}` for a
319	tenant that has never declared one. The stored table lists only the types
320	the declaration named; types left at the default are not copied into it.
321	
322	A tenant can also remove the table it declared, on the same path with the
323	`DELETE` method and the same calling shape as the other price writes:
324	
325	```http
326	DELETE /prices
327	Idempotency-Key: price-delete-1
328	X-Tenant-Id: acme
329	
330	{}
331	```
332	
333	The body must be exactly an empty object; a non-empty or non-object body,
334	an unknown field, or a non-finite value is a `400 validation_error` that
335	touches no price table. The delete removes the table as a whole and leaves
336	no partial write: it is atomic with the declaration and the read, so a
337	concurrent reader sees either the complete old table or no table at all.
338	After it succeeds the tenant no longer holds a declared table, and both the
339	delete response and the following read give the definite empty result
340	`{"prices":null}`. Deleting the table of a tenant that never declared one
341	returns that same definite empty result rather than an error. The delete
342	rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken before it was
343	made; afterward both the bill and the bucketed bill price every type at the
344	built-in default, each line still giving the metered type, the actual
345	`unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent `subtotal`.
346	
347	The declaration and the delete follow the same idempotency rules as every
348	other write: the `Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same
349	declaration or the same delete with the same key returns the first result
350	and performs no second replacement or removal, and reusing a key for
351	another operation — including another price declaration or a price delete
352	— in the same tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the tenant's price
353	table unchanged. Price tables are scoped per tenant like everything else: a
354	tenant can never read or delete another's declaration, and another tenant's
355	declaration or deletion never affects this tenant's bill amounts.
356	
357	The bill and the bucketed bill price with the price table in effect **at
358	query time**: a named type uses the tenant's declared price and every other
359	type uses the built-in default. Each returned line still gives the metered
360	type, the actual `unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent
361	`subtotal`, and the total is exactly the sum of the listed subtotals; types
362	with no matching record are still omitted rather than listed at zero. A
363	declaration affects only later queries — it neither rewrites recorded usage
364	nor revises historical bills — changes no metering, and leaves the bill and
365	usage queries read-only. A delete affects only later queries in the same
366	way: the table is removed as a whole, later bills fall back to the
367	built-in defaults, and recorded usage and already-taken bills stay exactly
368	as they were.
369	
370	### Price-table change history
371	
372	Every successful price-table declaration or delete leaves one change record,
373	so a caller can see exactly when each repricing and each table removal took
374	effect. A separate entry point returns the tenant's change history:
375	
376	```http
377	GET /prices/history?limit=50
378	X-Tenant-Id: acme
379	```
380	
381	Returns `{"history":[...]}` with the records in ascending order of occurrence
382	time; records sharing one instant are ordered by a stable ascending sequence.
383	Each record is:
384	
385	```json
386	{"sequence":7,"action":"declare","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z","snapshot":{"execution_started":200}}
387	```
388	
389	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant,
390	  shared across every kind of price change. It identifies the record across
391	  every query and is never renumbered by a filter or a page;
392	- `action` is `declare` for a price-table declaration or `delete` for a
393	  removal;
394	- `occurred_at` is the moment the change took effect, an ISO-8601 UTC string
395	  ending in `Z`;
396	- `snapshot` is the table in effect after the change. A declaration's
397	  snapshot is the type-to-unit-price map that took effect, listing only the
398	  types that declaration named and in ascending type-identifier order; a
399	  delete's snapshot is `null`.
400	
401	The history record is written atomically with the change it describes, in the
402	same transaction as the price-table write, so a reader always sees the table
403	and its history agree and a rejected declaration, delete, or idempotency-key
404	conflict leaves no record. Repeating an idempotent declaration or delete with
405	the same key returns the first result and appends no second record; reusing a
406	key for another operation is the usual `409 conflict` and, again, writes no
407	history. A delete of a table that was never declared still succeeds and still
408	leaves its own `delete` record (with a `null` snapshot), exactly as it returns
409	the definite empty result for the table itself.
410	
411	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
412	`{"history":[]}`, never an error. The response is one line of compact JSON
413	with the record keys in the order above, full number precision preserved, and
414	a single trailing newline, like every other JSON endpoint.
415	
416	The endpoint accepts an optional action filter, the same optional closed time
417	window the per-record usage query accepts, plus cursor pagination:
418	
419	```http
420	GET /prices/history?action=declare,delete&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
421	```
422	
423	- `action` names one action or a comma-separated set of them (`declare` and
424	  `delete`); only records whose action is in the set are returned. A single
425	  value needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
426	  action is a `400 validation_error`; when `action` is absent every change is
427	  returned;
428	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
429	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
430	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
431	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing
432	  and the definite empty list is returned;
433	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
434	  contains more than that many records;
435	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
436	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
437	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
438	- the action filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
439	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
440	
441	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `action` entry, a
442	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
443	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
444	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
445	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
446	appends no history, changes no price table, and changes no metering, usage,
447	bill, quota, or scheduling conclusion. History follows the usual tenant
448	isolation, so another tenant's changes are never visible under any action
449	filter, window, or page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and
450	recovery leave every recorded sequence, time, and snapshot unchanged.
451	
452	### Usage metering and billing
453	
454	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
455	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
456	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
457	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
458	metered action types are:
459	
460	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
461	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
462	  definition;
463	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
464	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
465	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
466	  `schedule_triggered`;
467	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
468	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
469	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
470	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
471	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
472	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
473	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
474	  meters nothing.
475	
476	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
477	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
478	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
479	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
480	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
481	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
482	
483	```http
484	GET /usage
485	X-Tenant-Id: acme
486	```
487	
488	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
489	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
490	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
491	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
492	
493	```http
494	GET /bill
495	X-Tenant-Id: acme
496	```
497	
498	Returns the per-type bill:
499	
500	```json
501	{"bill":{"items":[
502	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
503	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
504	],"total":2100}}
505	```
506	
507	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
508	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
509	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
510	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`. The price used per type is
511	the tenant's declared price when its price table names that type and the
512	built-in default otherwise, read from the table in effect at query time (see
513	[Tenant price tables](#tenant-price-tables)); tenants with no declaration are
514	billed byte for byte as before.
515	
516	Both endpoints accept the same optional query parameters the events and
517	metrics queries accept: an optional metered-type filter and an ISO-8601 UTC
518	timestamp window, each timestamp ending in `Z`, plus an optional fixed time
519	bucket:
520	
521	```http
522	GET /usage?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
523	GET /bill?type=execution_started&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
524	X-Tenant-Id: acme
525	```
526	
527	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them; only
528	  records whose type is in the set are counted. A single identifier needs no
529	  comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered type is a
530	  `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is counted, exactly
531	  as before;
532	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on each usage record's
533	  occurrence time: a record whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted.
534	  When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting
535	  both returns exactly the cumulative result above;
536	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
537	  parameter is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing;
538	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
539	  simply contains no records. Usage then reports the definite empty result
540	  `{"usage":[]}`, and the bill reports an empty `items` list with a `total` of
541	  `0`.
542	
543	The type filter and the time window apply together as an intersection: a
544	record is counted only when its type is named **and** its occurrence time is
545	in the window. A type the filter names but that has no matching record is
546	omitted rather than reported at zero, so a filter that matches nothing gives
547	the same definite empty results as an empty window: `{"usage":[]}` for usage
548	and an empty `items` list with a `total` of `0` for the bill.
549	
550	Both endpoints also accept an optional `bucket` parameter for a fixed-bucket
551	trend summary, so callers never have to pull records and group them
552	themselves:
553	
554	```http
555	GET /usage?bucket=hour&since=2026-09-26T00:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-27T00:00:00.000Z
556	GET /bill?bucket=day&type=execution_started
557	X-Tenant-Id: acme
558	```
559	
560	- `bucket` is exactly `hour` or `day`: `hour` buckets start on the UTC hour
561	  and `day` buckets at UTC midnight, both aligned solely to UTC. An empty or
562	  any other value is a `400 validation_error`, exactly like a repeated
563	  parameter or an unknown query parameter;
564	- when `bucket` is present, usage returns
565	  `{"usage_buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T08:00:00Z","usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}, ...]}`:
566	  the buckets with at least one matching record, in ascending bucket-start
567	  order. Each entry gives its `bucket_start` first — an ISO-8601 UTC string
568	  ending in `Z` at the hour or midnight — followed by `usage`, the per-type
569	  counts inside that bucket in ascending type-identifier order; a type with no
570	  record in the bucket is omitted;
571	- when `bucket` is present, the bill returns
572	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T00:00:00Z","items":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100}, ...],"subtotal":100}, ...],"total":100}}`.
573	  Buckets appear in ascending bucket-start order; each bucket's `items` stay
574	  sorted by ascending type identifier, each line giving the filtered count,
575	  the usual positive-integer `unit_price`, and an integer-cent `subtotal` of
576	  the two, and a type with no matching record is omitted rather than reported
577	  at zero. Each bucket also carries its own `subtotal`, and the window
578	  `total` is exactly the sum of the listed per-bucket subtotals, all amounts
579	  integer cents;
580	- a bucket that holds no matching record never appears, so an empty tenant, a
581	  window with `since` later than `until`, or a filter that matches nothing
582	  returns the definite empty bucket lists `{"usage_buckets":[]}` and
583	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[],"total":0}` — never an error, with the empty bill's
584	  total at `0`;
585	- bucketing applies together with the type filter and the time window as an
586	  intersection: a bucket holds only records whose occurrence time is in the
587	  closed window **and** whose type the filter names. The window keeps its
588	  closed endpoints, its open bounds when either side is omitted, and the
589	  existing rule for when a record's instant falls in it; buckets are simply
590	  the same matching records rolled up to their UTC bucket;
591	- the bucketed queries are read-only like the others: they append no usage
592	  records, change no metering basis or prices, and never alter recorded usage
593	  or billing conclusions — under event replay or recovery the same window,
594	  type filter, and bucket always give the same answer;
595	- omitting `bucket` leaves both queries exactly as before: the same compact
596	  JSON responses with `usage` / `items` shapes, full float precision and the
597	  `-0.0` convention, byte for byte. The parameter introduces no second
598	  protocol and changes no entry point's existing behavior.
599	
600	Only records whose occurrence time falls in the window are counted. Within
601	the window the bill keeps the same basis as always: each present type reports
602	its filtered, windowed count, its usual `unit_price`, and a `subtotal` of the
603	two; items stay sorted by ascending type identifier, and a type with no
604	matching record is omitted rather than reported at zero. The bill's `total`
605	is exactly the sum of the subtotals of the listed items. The query is
606	read-only: it writes no usage records, changes no prices or metering
607	conclusions, and never alters already recorded usage — under event replay or
608	recovery the same window and type filter always give the same answer.
609	
610	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
611	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error` that reveals no usage. Usage and
612	bill data follow the usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see
613	another's records under any type filter or window, and another tenant's
614	records never affect this tenant's counts or totals.
615	
616	### Per-record usage history
617	
618	The cumulative usage query reports only per-type totals. A separate endpoint
619	returns the individual usage records themselves, so each billed action can be
620	checked against the moment it occurred:
621	
622	```http
623	GET /usage/records?limit=50
624	X-Tenant-Id: acme
625	```
626	
627	Returns `{"records":[...]}` with the matching records in ascending order of
628	occurrence time; records sharing one instant are ordered by ascending
629	sequence. Each record is:
630	
631	```json
632	{"sequence":7,"type":"execution_started","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z"}
633	```
634	
635	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant. It
636	  identifies the record across every query and is never renumbered by a
637	  filter or a page;
638	- `type` is the metered action type;
639	- `occurred_at` is the record's occurrence time as an ISO-8601 UTC string
640	  ending in `Z`.
641	
642	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
643	`{"records":[]}`, never an error. The response ends with a single newline,
644	like every other JSON endpoint.
645	
646	The endpoint accepts an optional metered-type filter, the same optional
647	closed time window the events and usage queries accept, plus cursor
648	pagination:
649	
650	```http
651	GET /usage/records?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
652	```
653	
654	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them;
655	  only records whose type is in the set are returned. A single identifier
656	  needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered
657	  type is a `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is
658	  returned, exactly as before;
659	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
660	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
661	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
662	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches
663	  nothing and the definite empty list is returned;
664	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
665	  contains more than that many records;
666	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
667	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
668	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
669	- the type filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
670	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
671	
672	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `type` entry, a
673	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
674	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
675	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
676	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
677	appends no usage records, writes no events, and changes no metering, prices,
678	quotas, or billing conclusions. Records follow the usual tenant isolation, so
679	another tenant's records are never visible under any type filter, window, or
680	page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and recovery leave every

683	### Operational metrics
684	
685	```http
686	GET /metrics
687	X-Tenant-Id: acme
688	```
689	
690	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
691	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
692	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
693	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
694	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
695	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
696	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
697	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
698	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
699	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
700	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
701	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
702	
703	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
704	timestamp ending in `Z`:
705	
706	```http
707	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
708	X-Tenant-Id: acme
709	```
710	
711	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
712	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
713	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
714	  counts every recorded fact;
715	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
716	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
717	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
718	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
719	  result.
720	
721	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
722	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
723	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
724	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
725	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
726	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
727	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
728	completion or termination event.
729	
730	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
731	
732	```http
733	GET /metrics/export
734	X-Tenant-Id: acme
735	```
736	
737	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
738	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
739	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
740	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
741	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
742	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
743	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
744	
745	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
746	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
747	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
748	ordered by ascending label value:
749	
750	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
751	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
752	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
753	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
754	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
755	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
756	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
757	  unlabeled scalar samples.
758	
759	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
760	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
761	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
762	ends with a single newline.
763	
764	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
765	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
766	failures, and schedule triggers:
767	
768	```json
769	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
770	```
771	
772	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
773	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
774	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
775	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
776	  ended for that reason.
777	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
778	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
779	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
780	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
781	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
782	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
783	  another attempt, per node identifier.
784	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
785	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
786	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
787	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
788	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
789	
790	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
791	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
792	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
793	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
794	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
795	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.

805	### Create a workflow
806	
807	```http
808	POST /workflows
809	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
810	
811	{
812	  "id": "order-flow",
813	  "nodes": [
814	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
815	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
816	  ]
817	}
818	```
819	
820	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
821	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
822	
823	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
824	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
825	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
826	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
827	
828	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
829	
830	```json
831	{
832	  "id": "order-flow",
833	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
834	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
835	}
836	```
837	
838	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
839	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
840	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
841	
842	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
843	
844	```json
845	{
846	  "id": "nightly-orders",
847	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
848	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
849	}
850	```
851	
852	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
853	
854	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
855	
856	```json
857	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
858	```
859	
860	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
861	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
862	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
863	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
864	`false`.
865	
866	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
867	
868	```json
869	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
870	```
871	
872	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
873	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
874	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
875	dependencies of its successors.
876	
877	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
878	
879	```json
880	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
881	```
882	
883	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
884	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
885	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
886	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
887	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
888	`retries_exhausted`.
889	
890	A task may instead declare an approval point:
891	
892	```json
893	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
894	```
895	
896	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
897	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
898	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
899	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
900	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
901	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
902	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
903	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
904	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
905	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
906	move the task.
907	
908	### Submit an approval decision
909	
910	```http
911	POST /executions/run-1/decision
912	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
913	
914	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
915	```
916	
917	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
918	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
919	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
920	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
921	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
922	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
923	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
924	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
925	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
926	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
927	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
928	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
929	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
930	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
931	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
932	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
933	404.
934	
935	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
936	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
937	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
938	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
939	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
940	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
941	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
942	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
943	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
944	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
945	shape and event stream.
946	
947	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
948	segment:
949	
950	```json
951	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
952	```
953	
954	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
955	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
956	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
957	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
958	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
959	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
960	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
961	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
962	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
963	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
964	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
965	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
966	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
967	loop node instead).
968	
969	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
970	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
971	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
972	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
973	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
974	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
975	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
976	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
977	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
978	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
979	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
980	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
981	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
982	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
983	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
984	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
985	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
986	belong only to their iterations.
987	
988	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
989	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
990	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
991	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
992	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
993	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
994	exactly.
995	
996	### Dynamic map nodes
997	
998	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
999	recorded array:
1000	
1001	```json
1002	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
1003	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
1004	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
1005	```
1006	
1007	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
1008	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
1009	
1010	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
1011	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
1012	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
1013	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
1014	  the same path syntax as a condition.
1015	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
1016	  expand.
1017	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
1018	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
1019	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
1020	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
1021	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
1022	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
1023	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
1024	
1025	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
1026	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
1027	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
1028	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
1029	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
1030	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
1031	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
1032	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
1033	overwrite another instance.
1034	
1035	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
1036	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
1037	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
1038	become available in the usual way.
1039	
1040	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
1041	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
1042	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
1043	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
1044	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
1045	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
1046	
1047	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
1048	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
1049	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
1050	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
1051	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
1052	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
1053	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
1054	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
1055	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
1056	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
1057	
1058	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
1059	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
1060	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
1061	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
1062	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
1063	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
1064	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
1065	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
1066	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
1067	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
1068	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
1069	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
1070	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
1071	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
1072	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
1073	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
1074	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
1075	
1076	### Maps inside loop bodies
1077	
1078	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
1079	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
1080	other body member:
1081	
1082	```json
1083	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
1084	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
1085	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
1086	```
1087	
1088	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
1089	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
1090	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
1091	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
1092	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
1093	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
1094	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
1095	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
1096	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
1097	
1098	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
1099	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
1100	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
1101	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
1102	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
1103	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
1104	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
1105	influence from the iteration number.
1106	
1107	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
1108	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
1109	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
1110	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
1111	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
1112	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
1113	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
1114	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
1115	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
1116	
1117	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
1118	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
1119	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
1120	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
1121	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
1122	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
1123	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
1124	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
1125	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
1126	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
1127	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
1128	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
1129	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
1130	
1131	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
1132	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
1133	
1134	### Delete and modify expanded instances
1135	
1136	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
1137	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
1138	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
1139	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
1140	
1141	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
1142	that has permanently failed:
1143	
1144	```http
1145	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
1146	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
1147	
1148	{}
1149	```
1150	
1151	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
1152	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
1153	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
1154	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
1155	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
1156	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
1157	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
1158	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
1159	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
1160	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
1161	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
1162	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
1163	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
1164	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
1165	
1166	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
1167	before it is worked:
1168	
1169	```http
1170	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
1171	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
1172	
1173	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
1174	```
1175	
1176	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
1177	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
1178	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
1179	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
1180	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
1181	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
1182	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
1183	is stored verbatim.
1184	
1185	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
1186	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
1187	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
1188	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
1189	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
1190	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
1191	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
1192	
1193	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
1194	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
1195	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
1196	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
1197	carries no loop context.
1198	
1199	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
1200	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
1201	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
1202	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
1203	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
1204	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
1205	first result and appends no second event.
1206	
1207	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
1208	
1209	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
1210	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
1211	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
1212	  and `iteration`;
1213	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
1214	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
1215	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
1216	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
1217	
1218	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
1219	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
1220	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
1221	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
1222	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
1223	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
1224	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
1225	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
1226	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
1227	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
1228	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
1229	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
1230	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
1231	
1232	### Re-expand a dynamic node
1233	
1234	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
1235	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
1236	
1237	```http
1238	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
1239	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
1240	
1241	{}
1242	```
1243	
1244	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
1245	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
1246	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
1247	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
1248	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
1249	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
1250	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
1251	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
1252	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
1253	bounds start from zero.
1254	
1255	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
1256	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
1257	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
1258	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
1259	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
1260	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
1261	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
1262	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
1263	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
1264	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
1265	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
1266	expansion.
1267	
1268	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
1269	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
1270	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
1271	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
1272	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
1273	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
1274	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
1275	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
1276	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1277	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
1278	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
1279	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
1280	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
1281	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
1282	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
1283	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
1284	an instance that stayed deleted.
1285	
1286	### Workflow versions
1287	
1288	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
1289	
1290	```json
1291	{
1292	  "id": "order-flow",
1293	  "version": "2026-09-25",
1294	  "nodes": [
1295	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
1296	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
1297	  ]
1298	}
1299	```
1300	
1301	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
1302	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
1303	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
1304	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
1305	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
1306	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
1307	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
1308	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
